# The two case studies {#the-four-cases .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Section 3
:::

::: notes
This section brings the programme down to the workshop's two case studies, each a claim that went through the robustness study and, to different degrees, through the rest of SCORE, while further case studies are in preparation. We read the two claims as the analysts received them, then the conclusions of the five analysts of each claim side by side, and then the record of each case study across the three Rs. Your own case study is one of the two, and since you meet it properly on the second day, the aim for now is only to place it beside the other.
:::

## The two claims {#the-four-claims .smaller}

::: {.fs-75}
| Case study | The study | The claim, as the robustness study gave it |
|:----|:-------------|:-------------|
| Housing and racial bias | A field experiment of 2017: one email to each of about a thousand public housing authorities in the United States, signed with names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic sender | "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts" |
| Europeanisation and the economy | An analysis of 2016 of sixteen Eurobarometer waves, 2004 to 2013, in 27 member states of the European Union | "... poor economic performances ... decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" |
:::

::: {.src}
@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, abstract; @Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 619.
:::

::: notes
These are the two claims in the form in which the robustness study handed them to the analysts, with the dots of the lead team left in. The Housing claim comes from an experiment, emails to public housing authorities in the United States that differed only in the name that signed them, and the Europeanisation claim from sixteen waves of the Eurobarometer. The claims are worth reading for what they leave out as much as for what they say: the Housing claim, for instance, states a direction and no size, because an ellipsis removed the twenty percentage points of the abstract.
:::

## The conclusions of the analysts {#the-conclusions-of-the-analysts}

```{r}
#| label: case-conclusions
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3
# The Task 1 conclusions of the five analysts of the robustness study for each
# case study, as the page score.qmd of this site states them (section "The case
# studies in the record"), from the facts file of each case study. One tile per
# analyst, in no particular order within a case study.
conclusions <- tibble::tribble(
  ~case,             ~conclusion,                  ~n,
  "Housing",         "Evidence for the claim",     3,
  "Housing",         "No evidence either way",     2,
  "Europeanisation", "Evidence for the claim",     5
) |>
  tidyr::uncount(n) |>
  dplyr::mutate(analyst = dplyr::row_number(), .by = case) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    case = factor(case, levels = rev(c("Housing", "Europeanisation"))),
    conclusion = factor(conclusion, levels = c("Evidence for the claim",
                                               "No evidence either way"))
  )

ggplot2::ggplot(conclusions, ggplot2::aes(analyst, case, fill = conclusion)) +
  ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 3, width = 0.96, height = 0.82) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c(ncl_blue, grey_mid), name = NULL) +
  # without the white border of the tiles, which would cover the legend keys
  ggplot2::guides(fill = ggplot2::guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = NA))) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(add = 0.05)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(16) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom",
                 legend.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 13, colour = ink),
                 legend.key.size = ggplot2::unit(1.1, "lines"),
                 panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank(),
                 axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_blank(),
                 axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink, size = 17))
```

::: {.small}
The four partial correlations recorded for the Housing analysts run from 0.143 to 0.196 in absolute value, although the analysts split on the conclusion. Every analyst upheld the Europeanisation claim, while the correlations recorded for its five reanalyses run from −0.006 to −0.452.
:::

::: {.src}
The Task 1 conclusions recorded in the robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], as the page SCORE and the opening page of the workshop's website state them.
:::

::: notes
Each row is one case study and each tile one analyst, coloured by the conclusion recorded in the first task. The Housing claim split three to two, with the other two analysts finding evidence neither way, while all five analysts upheld the Europeanisation claim. Agreement on the conclusion, however, is a different matter from agreement on the number. The Housing analysts, who split on the conclusion, recorded four correlations between about 0.14 and 0.20 in absolute value, while the correlations recorded for the Europeanisation analysts, who all upheld the claim, span nearly two orders of magnitude, for the reason shown by the slide on what the conversion assumes.
:::

## The two case studies in the record {#the-four-cases-in-the-record .smaller}

::: {.fs-75}
| Case study | Reproduction | Robustness | Replication |
|:----|:----------|:---------|:----------|
| Housing | never attempted, although the data and code are public | 3 of the 5 analysts for the claim, 2 neither way | a new preregistered experiment with 3,050 housing authorities found no significant gap |
| Europeanisation | two attempts from the original materials, neither successful | all 5 for the claim | on later Eurobarometer waves, judged not successful |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Read across the rows. The Europeanisation claim, upheld by every analyst, could be neither reproduced nor replicated, while the Housing claim, upheld by three of its five analysts, did not replicate in a new experiment.
:::

::: {.src}
The page SCORE on the workshop's website, from the facts file of each case study.
:::

::: notes
This is the whole record across the three Rs. In the reproduction column, the Housing reproduction was never attempted although everything needed for it was public, and both attempts on the Europeanisation paper failed. [advance] Read across the rows, the Europeanisation claim, upheld by every one of its analysts, could be neither reproduced from its original materials nor replicated on later waves of its survey, while the Housing claim, upheld by three of its five analysts, did not replicate in a new preregistered experiment with 3,050 housing authorities. Two case studies are far too few for a conclusion about the literature, but they show, one case at a time, why the workshop keeps the three questions apart.
:::
